chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ibn Fazzal, from Abu Jameela, from Muhammad ibn Humran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When any one of you intends a good deed or maintaining kinship ties, there are two devils with him, one on his right and one on his left; so let him hasten [to act] so that they do not prevent him from that.

key_terms.صِلَةٍ: Maintaining kinship ties or social connections
key_terms.لَا يَكُفَّاهُ: So that they do not prevent or restrain him
key_terms.لِيُبَادِرْ: Let him hasten or be quick

ai.seo_question: How do devils try to stop good deeds according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this hadith to emphasize the spiritual urgency of 'hastening' (tabarru') in good deeds, a key concept in Shia ethics where immediate action prevents the devil from exploiting hesitation. The presence of two devils—one for each side of the heart—symbolizes the dual nature of internal distractions, urging the believer to act decisively before doubt or procrastination takes hold.
